hook.text: For over a thousand years, Catholic mass was in Latin. Most worshippers understood nothing.

buildup.text: Sacred languages—Latin, Sanskrit, Classical Arabic—are kept unchanged to preserve divine authority.

discovery.text: Hebrew was a dead liturgical language for 1,700 years until Eliezer Ben-Yehuda revived it for daily speech.

twist.text: Keeping scripture in an elite language gives clergy a monopoly on interpretation—and therefore on truth.

climax.text: Martin Luther's German Bible broke that monopoly. Within a century, Europe was reshaped by the Reformation.

punchline.text: Translation is always a political act.

quiz.question: Who revived Hebrew as a spoken language?

details.summary: Sacred languages — Sanskrit, Arabic, Hebrew, Latin, Pali — hold special status as languages of divine communication. Arabic is considered the literal language of God's revelation in Islam. Sanskrit mantras must be pronounced exactly or lose their power.
details.whyItMatters: Sacred languages demonstrate the deepest connection between language and power — when a language is believed to be God's own medium, changing it becomes blasphemy.
takeaways: Arabic in the Quran is considered God's literal language
Sanskrit mantras require exact pronunciation for spiritual efficacy
Hebrew was revived as a spoken language after 1,700 years of sacred-only use

faq.question: Why is Arabic considered sacred?
faq.answer: Muslims believe the Quran is God's literal speech delivered in Arabic to the Prophet Muhammad. Unlike the Bible (considered inspired but written by humans), the Quran is held to be the exact words of God.

faq.question: How was Hebrew revived?
faq.answer: Hebrew had not been a spoken everyday language for about 1,700 years — it survived only in religious texts and prayer. Eliezer Ben-Yehuda led a 19th-century revival movement, creating new words for modern concepts, raising the first modern native Hebrew speaker (his son), and advocating Hebrew-only.
